turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Friday, September 4th. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex — Nvidia just spent 12.93 billion dollars buying the open-source AI world's favorite platform, and Beijing's rare-earth suppliers just stopped shipping to the US without telling anyone. Let's get into it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Start in the Himalayas, because the death toll from that Nepal-China flood disaster just jumped hard. Nepal's disaster authority now says 1,114 dead nationally, plus 16 confirmed on the Chinese side — call it 1,130 total, up from the roughly 389 dead we had last week.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And that's with 4,500 people still missing across both countries. Nearly 12,000 have been rescued in Nepal alone as the search enters a second week. This is the kind of story where the first-week numbers were always going to be wrong — glacial-lake outburst floods bury bodies under debris fields that take weeks to clear, not days.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Any sense of whether the toll keeps climbing from here, or are we near the ceiling?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: With 4,500 still missing and search-and-rescue only now reaching some of the more remote valleys, I'd expect at least a few hundred more confirmed dead before this stabilizes. It's already one of the deadliest glacial-flood events on record for the region.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Different kind of story out of London — Andy Burnham had his first Prime Minister's Questions yesterday, going after Kemi Badenoch on tax and borrowing. Same day, Nigel Farage got sworn back into the Commons after winning the Clacton by-election.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And immediately got accused of breaching parliamentary rules on his first day back — so business as usual for Farage. Burnham's only been PM since July 20th when he replaced Starmer, so this was genuinely his first real test at the dispatch box.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And in Niger, a journalist has vanished. Moussa Kaka — director of Radio Télévision Saraounia, former RFI correspondent — disappeared after leaving his Niamey office the evening of August 31st, days after the coup attempt the junta says it put down with Russian military help.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Human Rights Watch called it a likely forced disappearance on September 3rd; Reporters Without Borders is demanding an urgent probe. Kaka was already arrested and detained back in October on vague "public order" charges, so this fits a pattern, not an isolated incident.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What does it say about the junta's confidence right now?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A government that just survived a coup attempt with foreign military backing doesn't usually go after a single radio director unless it's nervous about the narrative he controls. Disappearing a well-known journalist days after a failed coup is a signal to every other independent outlet in Niamey, not an isolated grudge.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Worth noting Kaka isn't a fringe figure either — he spent years as an RFI correspondent, which means international wire services already have a relationship with him and are more likely to keep this story alive than they would for a purely local reporter.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Big one — Nvidia is buying Hugging Face for 12.93 billion dollars. 11.9 billion to shareholders, another billion in retention equity for employees who join Nvidia.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's Nvidia's second-largest acquisition ever, after the roughly 20 billion dollar Groq assets deal. And the number that matters here isn't the price — it's what they're buying: 3 million models, a million apps, over 18 million developers on the platform. That's the open-source AI commons, and Nvidia just bought it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Huang's saying it stays open, no Nvidia compute lock-in. Do you believe that?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: I believe it stays open in name — walking that back would torch the platform's entire value. But "open and owned by your biggest hardware supplier" is a different thing than "open and neutral." Every model card, every benchmark leaderboard on Hugging Face now sits inside Nvidia's house. Deal's expected to close in the first half of 2027.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Broadcom's the other one — record Q3 revenue, 29.6 billion dollars, up 86% year-over-year, and the stock still dropped about 3%.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: AI semiconductor revenue alone was 16.7 billion, up 221%, now 56% of total revenue. Net income more than tripled to 13.09 billion. The drop is entirely about the Q4 guide — 34.8 billion revenue, 21.7 billion of that AI — which investors read as underwhelming against expectations that had gotten completely unmoored from reality.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Germany may finally let UniCredit buy Commerzbank. Reuters reporting this morning that Berlin has opened direct talks with the Italian bank after years of resistance.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: UniCredit already has access to nearly half of Commerzbank's shares — 49.65%. And Commerzbank's own CEO, Bettina Orlopp, has basically said she won't stay if she can't cut a deal with UniCredit and whatever board it installs. That's a CEO signaling the fight is over before the paperwork is.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Japan — its 10-year government bond yield hit 3% this week. First time since 1996.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the headline everyone's going to miss the significance of. The yield's more than tripled in two years, and Japan's own FY26 budget assumed a 3% long-term rate for debt-servicing costs — so this isn't just a market move, it's a budget assumption getting breached in real time. The 20-year hit 3.885%, also a level last seen in 1996, and the 30-year was closing in on a record high near 4.18%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Markets tab has the full board today, so let's not read it all — Thursday was a broad rally, S&P up about 1.06%, Dow up 1.18%, Nasdaq up 1.4%, on dovish comments from a Fed governor and falling yields. Real move, just short of screaming-headline territory.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The thing that actually matters is what's landing this morning — August's jobs report. Payrolls up only 22,000 against a 75,000 estimate, unemployment ticking up to 4.3%. That's a real labor-market-weakening print, not noise.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So which story wins — the dovish Fed tilt that rallied stocks Thursday, or a jobs miss that should worry people?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: They're actually the same story told from two different rooms. A soft labor market is exactly what gives the Fed cover to cut, which is why gold's up almost 1.4% — haven demand ahead of a print that traders were clearly positioned for. The tension is whether "labor market weak enough to justify a cut" quietly becomes "labor market weak enough to worry about a recession," and that line moves fast once you're on the wrong side of it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Anything else worth flagging?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Just that the dollar's drifted lower — DXY down slightly — and the peso's basically flat against it. Everything else is drift. Full board's on the Markets tab if you want the granular levels.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Alright, Deep Dive. New York City just banned generative AI for its youngest students — and this is worth sitting with, because it's the broadest school AI moratorium in the country.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Mayor Mamdani and the new Schools Chancellor, Kamar Samuels, announced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI tools for grades pre-K through 8 — that's around 600,000 kids, two-thirds of the district's total enrollment. Paired with hard screen-time caps: 30 minutes a day for grades 3 through 5, 45 minutes for middle school, and a full ban on individual devices below third grade.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: High schoolers still get access?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Restricted access, through five pilot programs — so the district isn't saying AI has no place in education, it's saying young kids specifically shouldn't have unsupervised access to it. Mamdani's exact line was, "Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Here's what makes this genuinely interesting rather than just another policy announcement — NYC already did this dance once. They banned ChatGPT district-wide back in 2023, then lifted the ban months later, saying publicly that they'd "overlooked the potential" of the technology.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So this is the second reversal, and it's broader and under entirely new leadership. That whiplash tells you something real — nobody, including the people running one of the largest school systems in the country, actually has a stable answer to what AI access should look like for children. They tried "banned," tried "open," and are now trying "banned again, but with data behind it this time."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's actually driving the reversal, beyond vibes?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: City Council's education chair, Eric Dinowitz, says DOE is directly responding to pressure from public hearings — parents and teachers pushing back hard enough that the political calculus flipped. But notably, key implementation details — which specific tools are actually covered by the ban — were still unclear days before the school year started. That's not a fully baked policy, it's a fast reaction to political pressure that's going to get worked out in real time.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why should someone who doesn't have kids in NYC public schools care about this?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because it's the first large-scale, real-world experiment in hard limits on AI adoption applied to exactly the population least equipped to self-regulate use — children. Every ed-tech company selling into K-12 has been betting the arrow only points toward more AI integration. NYC just showed the arrow can point backward, twice, in under three years. If a coalition of parents and teachers can reverse policy at the largest school district in the country, that's a template other cities are going to notice.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Backup angle we didn't run with today but is worth a mention — Terence Tao published an essay on AI in mathematics research that's been circulating hard in academic circles. His actual policy proposal: he'd block publication of a paper if the authors can't give an expert-level talk defending their own AI-assisted result.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which reframes the whole debate usefully — away from "how capable is the AI" and toward "can the human still verify and own what it produced." Same underlying anxiety as the NYC story, just playing out in a research lab instead of a third-grade classroom.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Energy — starting with the tariff data. There are now 65 state-level large-load tariffs on the books, and a Latitude Media and RMI analysis just mapped the common ratepayer-protection terms across all of them.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Five recurring mechanisms: minimum contract terms, a lot of them 15-plus years; minimum monthly billing demand — take-or-pay at 75 to 90% of contracted capacity; collateral requirements; exit fees; and capacity reassignment rights. Utility data-center capex pipelines now total over a trillion dollars across five years, so these aren't boilerplate clauses, they're the difference between hyperscalers actually paying their way and residential ratepayers eating stranded costs.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which of those five is the one to watch?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exit fees and reassignment rights, because those are exactly what gets watered down in PUC negotiations when a utility wants the deal signed badly enough. That's the Georgia Power and Duke Florida pattern — now generalized across 65 states instead of two headline fights.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there a reason a utility would want to water those terms down, beyond just wanting the deal?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Competition between states for the same hyperscaler campus. If Virginia's exit fees are ironclad and Ohio's are negotiable, the marginal data-center project goes to Ohio — so every state PUC is under quiet pressure to be the friendlier jurisdiction, which is exactly the race-to-the-bottom dynamic ratepayer advocates are worried about.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: SpaceX is getting into gas turbines now?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Vertically integrating into turbine components, specifically. They're building a foundry in Bastrop, Texas to cast single-crystal nickel-superalloy blades and vanes — the same casting process used for Raptor engine turbopumps, now applied to natural-gas power turbines. Musk's claiming up to 18 months off turbine lead times.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's the actual bottleneck everyone in your world keeps talking about.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It is — GE Vernova, Siemens, Mitsubishi have had gas turbine order books stretching years out. TechCrunch's counter-read is worth noting: faster turbine deployment for AI load means faster local emissions and permitting fights, not fewer of them — you've just moved the constraint downstream. But strategically this is the same logic as Nvidia taking equity stakes in powered land — control your own bottleneck instead of waiting in someone else's queue, just applied one layer further upstream, straight at the turbine oligopoly itself.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Before we move on — is there a read on whether these tariff terms are actually holding up load growth projections, or is it mostly paperwork?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's more than paperwork at this point. Several utilities have started tying their own generation build-out timelines directly to signed large-load contracts rather than forecasted demand — which means a slow tariff negotiation now delays real steel-in-the-ground decisions, not just billing terms. That's the shift practitioners should actually be watching.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There's also a battery storage angle on Trump's foreign-grid-equipment order.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, and this is a real update on a story we've already covered — BloombergNEF's analysis says the EO lands very unevenly. Transformers and switchgear are mostly insulated, because the US already sources those domestically or from non-Chinese suppliers. Battery storage is the exposed one — the US sources about 60% of lithium-ion cells from China.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Who actually gets hurt by that?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Projects that broke ground before the January 1st, 2026 Foreign-Entity-of-Concern compliance deadline but haven't reached commercial operation yet — they're caught mid-build with no clean supplier swap available. Expect near-term BESS delays and cancellations, and storage-backed data-center PPAs getting repriced to account for the risk.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And wind's having a rough quarter.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The pipeline's shrinking on two fronts at once. About 5 gigawatts of onshore wind got added in Q2, but the pipeline itself fell 4% quarter-over-quarter, and 44 gigawatts are stuck in Department of Defense review — that's radar interference concerns, not general permitting friction. Meanwhile wind PPA prices rose 5.5% quarter-over-quarter, 17.5% year-over-year, while solar PPA prices actually fell 4.8% from Q1.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So capital's just rotating.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Total clean-power pipeline — wind, solar, storage combined — is still up 11% year-over-year, over 200 gigawatts. But it's increasingly a solar-plus-storage-plus-gas story, not the "all of the above" narrative the industry likes to tell. Wind's getting specifically sidelined by a defense-review bottleneck nobody else in the stack is facing.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last one — something from an actual founder survey.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: CTVC and Elemental Impact surveyed over 100 climate-tech founders. The headline tension: 70% say equity is what would most accelerate their growth, but 73% say capital *structure*, not amount, is their top barrier — traditional VC just doesn't fit capital-intensive infrastructure timelines. And there's a sector split: 83% of nuclear founders say project-capital access improved this year, versus 64% of carbon-removal founders who say it got worse.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the mismatch they flagged?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Founders rank tech and scale-up risk as their top barrier — 77% at pre-commercial stage — then customer acquisition, then permitting. But their *policy* asks skew toward carbon pricing and stable tax credits, which doesn't actually address permitting or interconnection, the things actually slowing them down on the ground. Same edition had real deals too — Emerald AI, a grid-interactive data-center platform, raised 150 million in Series A; Apollo Atomics, a compact pressurized-water SMR, raised 26 million seed; Quaise Energy, which drills geothermal wells using millimeter-wave technology instead of conventional drill bits, closed a 46 million dollar Series B.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That policy-versus-reality mismatch feels like it applies well beyond climate tech.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It does — it's the classic gap between what founders lobby Washington for and what actually gets a project built. Tax credits move fast through Congress and make for a clean press release; permitting reform requires touching entrenched state and local review processes nobody wants to own. So the easy ask keeps winning the policy conversation even though it's not the bottleneck founders themselves say is holding them back.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Panahon na para sa Tagalog vocab. Dalawang salita ngayon, kapwa konektado sa balita tungkol sa implasyon sa Pilipinas.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Una, ang salitang "lumuwag." Ibig sabihin nito, gumaan o humupa nang bahagya — hindi biglaan, kundi unti-unting pagbaba ng tensyon o presyon.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tama. At may pinag-iba ito sa salitang "bumagsak," na natutunan na natin dati. Ang "bumagsak" ay biglaan at matindi — parang isang malakas na pagbagsak. Pero ang "lumuwag" ay mas mahinahon — parang isang bagay na dahan-dahang gumagaan, hindi bigla.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Halimbawa: "Lumuwag nang bahagya ang implasyon noong Agosto, mula 6.6% patungong 6.1%."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Eksakto — apat na buwan nang sunod-sunod na lumuluwag ang implasyon. Hindi ito isang biglaang pagbagsak, kundi mabagal at patuloy na pagpapagaan.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang pangalawang salita naman ay "pabigat." Ito ay pangngalan — ibig sabihin, dagdag na bigat o pasanin sa isang sitwasyon.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: At may pinag-iba rin ito sa salitang "pasanin," na natutunan na rin natin. Ang "pasanin" ay isang bagay na dala-dala mo — tungkulin, responsibilidad, parang bagahe sa likod. Pero ang "pabigat" ay mas pangkalahatan — isang bagay na nagpapabigat sa buong sitwasyon, hindi lang sa isang tao.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Halimbawa: "Malaking pabigat sa mga pamilya ang pagtaas ng presyo ng bigas nang 19.4%."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oo — kahit lumuluwag ang pangkalahatang implasyon, ang presyo ng bigas mismo ay tumataas pa rin nang malaki. Ito ang klase ng detalye na hindi mo makikita kung titignan mo lang ang pangkalahatang numero.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Bumagal ang implasyon sa 6.1% noong Agosto, ika-apat na buwan nang sunod-sunod na pagbaba mula sa 7.2% noong Abril.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Pero tumaas pa ang presyo ng bigas nang 19.4% — malaking pabigat ito sa gastusin ng bawat pamilya.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: At kahit lumuwag ang implasyon, mananatiling mas mataas ang average nito kumpara sa target ng BSP.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Okay, back to English for the rest. That well-milled rice price is now 56.29 pesos a kilo, up 19.6% year-over-year, and it alone contributed 1.3 percentage points to headline CPI. The January-through-August average is still 5.2%, above the BSP's 2-to-4% comfort ceiling.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The bigger story sitting underneath that is a growth downgrade — Moody's Analytics just cut its 2026 Philippine growth forecast to 3%, from 4%. That's below the Marcos administration's own already-downgraded target of 3.5 to 4.5%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's Moody's actual argument?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That the Philippines is missing the regional AI and data-center investment wave that's lifting Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia through semiconductor and data-center demand. Weak domestic consumption from still-elevated inflation compounds it — you're not getting the external tailwind other ASEAN economies are getting, and the internal demand engine is also underpowered.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: On the impeachment trial — any real movement, or just scheduling?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Mostly scheduling, but notable scheduling. Senate Presiding Officer Chiz Escudero announced whole-day hearings starting in October, then a suspension so the Senate can handle 2027 budget deliberations, before resuming November 9th and 16th. So the trial's no longer running as a straight sprint — it's now fragmented and competing directly with the budget calendar for floor time.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And there's a power story too — Enrique Razon's Primelectric signed an MOU with PEZA.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: To study building dedicated power distribution systems inside selected economic zones — this targets a genuinely long-standing investor complaint about ecozone power reliability. And separately, around 200,000 SOCOTECO II member-consumers start a four-weekend plebiscite this weekend on the Razon-Pacquiao "Ignite Power" takeover bid.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Skipping the PSEi today — no major move — and no weather story, since there's no active PAGASA signal, just routine monsoon rain.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: One more worth flagging on the ecozone story — the plebiscite matters beyond SOCOTECO itself. If member-consumers approve the Razon-Pacquiao takeover, it's a template for consolidating other struggling electric cooperatives under private capital, which the sector's needed for years given how many co-ops are undercapitalized for the load growth everyone's now planning around.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Two Mandarin words today, both tied to the China story coming up. First is a connective pattern: 之所以…是因为…, zhī suǒyǐ, shì yīnwèi.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's it actually doing that plain 因为 doesn't?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 因为 is the everyday word for "because" — perfectly fine in casual speech. 之所以…是因为… is 书面语, formal written register — it front-loads the result, then explains the cause. It's the pattern you'd actually read in a news analysis piece, not something you'd say ordering coffee.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Give me it in context.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 中国厂商之所以暗中停止对美国的稀土出货，是因为担心材料被转卖给受制裁的实体。Zhōngguó chǎngshāng zhī suǒyǐ ànzhōng tíngzhǐ duì Měiguó de xītǔ chūhuò, shì yīnwèi dānxīn cáiliào bèi zhuǎnmài gěi shòu zhìcái de shítǐ. "The reason Chinese suppliers quietly halted rare-earth shipments to the US is because they're worried the material will be resold to sanctioned entities."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And that sentence already has our second word buried in it — 暗中, àn zhōng.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, "covertly, secretly" — doing something without announcing it. The near-synonym is 偷偷, tōu tōu, which is the everyday spoken version — sneaking around, often a slightly petty or childish connotation, like sneaking a cookie.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: But 暗中 is a different register entirely.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Formal, strategic — used for states and corporations acting quietly, not people hiding candy. 供应商暗中拒绝了至少四批发货，却没有公开宣布。Gōngyìngshāng ànzhōng jùjuéle zhìshǎo sì pī fāhuò, què méiyǒu gōngkāi xuānbù. "Suppliers covertly refused at least four shipments, without publicly announcing it." Exactly the story we're about to get into.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 中国供应商之所以暗中停止对美国的稀土出货，是因为担心材料被转卖给受制裁的实体。The reason Chinese suppliers quietly halted rare-earth shipments to the US is because they're worried about re-export to sanctioned end users.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Walk me through the actual mechanics of this.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Several firms have refused at least four documented shipments since early August, when Beijing sanctioned the Responsible Business Alliance — a US supply-chain monitor — over exactly this re-export concern. Prices for yttrium, indium phosphide, and tungsten are all sitting near record highs. Yttrium specifically is a jet-engine thermal coating, so aerospace manufacturers are already warning about rationing and possible production pauses.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the timing isn't an accident.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: This lands three weeks before Xi's September 24th Washington visit. Rare-earth access is now squarely on the pre-summit agenda, and doing it quietly rather than announcing formal export curbs gives Beijing deniability and leverage at the same time — they can point to individual corporate caution rather than state policy, while still making the message land in every affected boardroom.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Art world — The Art Newspaper ran a sharp piece on August 1st about what they're calling the billionaire problem, and the numbers back it up.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Christie's and Sotheby's combined for roughly 10 billion dollars in first-half 2026 sales. Sotheby's hit 4.4 billion, a record; Christie's hit 4.5 billion, up 71%. Eight lots sold above 50 million dollars, against zero in that range the year before — led by Pollock's "Number 7A, 1948" at 181 million.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That sounds like a healthy recovery on paper.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It sounds like one, but nearly a third of that total volume came from single-owner billionaire collections. The Art Newspaper's actual argument is that this isn't a broad-based recovery in collecting — it's concentration. You've got a shrinking pool of trophy buyers propping up headline numbers that read as market health but really describe something closer to wealth concentration finding an outlet.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Different register — Frieze's September issue.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Sasha Frere-Jones profiles the composer and writer JJJJJerome Ellis ahead of a show at the Vienna Secession in Vienna — Ellis's work treats stuttering and disfluency itself as compositional material, not something to smooth over. That's now getting a major European institutional platform, which is a real statement about what counts as serious composition right now.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What makes that pairing work as a segment?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: They're both stories about what gets legitimized and by whom — one's about which art gets priced as trophy-grade by a shrinking billionaire class, the other's about which art gets institutionally validated by a major European venue. Same underlying question about gatekeeping, two completely different corners of the art world.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Same issue also has Cassie Packard writing on artists working through space-science philosophy — worth a mention?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Just a flag for anyone who wants the deeper read — it's less a single story and more a sign of where serious art criticism is spending its attention right now: not chasing market headlines, but tracking artists engaging seriously with scientific and philosophical material. That's the throughline across the whole issue.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Op-eds — Joseph Stiglitz has a piece in Project Syndicate arguing American global influence is fading, and that this is actually a good thing.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: His steelman: Trump and Bessent's escalating tariffs, secondary sanctions, dollar-weaponization threats aren't signs of strength, they're what powers reach for once persuasion and legitimacy have already eroded — coercion is a symptom of declining leverage, not a demonstration of it. And the multipolar world that results, he argues, is healthier — it forces burden-sharing and stops the rest of the world from being exposed to the whims of one erratic actor.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the hole in that?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Look at this week's own throughline — Hormuz incidents spreading across four countries, an oil-legitimacy trade in Venezuela, the PBOC struggling to manage a currency it can't fully control. A receding US hegemon doesn't obviously produce Stiglitz's calmer multipolarity. Historically, waning single-power orders — interwar Europe, the post-Ottoman Middle East — produce vacuums filled by regional powers with less capacity and less accountability to coordinate, not more of it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There's a second piece worth a mention — Jan-Werner Mueller on how the AfD operates.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: His argument is that populist parties win less through explicit policy argument than through aesthetics — style, meme culture, tone — letting voters absorb exclusionary politics without having to confront it as such. It's a real, underexamined mechanism, distinct from the standard "economic anxiety" explanation.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the counter?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The aesthetics framing risks being unfalsifiable and a bit elitist-coded — it can imply voters are simply being duped by branding, rather than making a legible judgment about immigration or crime or a mainstream party's own drift rightward. That's the exact "who gets to say what counts as real politics" gatekeeping that fuels support for parties like the AfD in the first place.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One good thing today, and it's a genuinely lovely one. Adam James — goes by Adzo, 23 years old, autistic and ADHD — went to Boomtown Festival in Hampshire, England, completely alone, hoping to make it as a drum-and-bass DJ.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And a group of strangers — Adam's dad calls them "the lads from Bristol" — just took him in. Camped with him, made sure he had, in his own words, the best weekend of his life.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: His dad posted a thank-you online and it went properly viral.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And here's the part that turns this from a nice moment into a real outcome — Boomtown has since booked Adam to actually DJ a set at next year's festival. So it's not just a warm story that ends with everyone going home; a group of strangers being kind to a lonely guy for one weekend genuinely changed the trajectory of his year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: No caveat needed on this one — just a good story to end the week on.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Sometimes that's the whole point — no analysis required, just a genuinely good weekend for someone who needed one.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's it for us — have a good Friday, and we'll see you Monday.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Take care, everyone.
